positions/ethiopian-canon/altNames/1: Narrower and broader canons of Ethiopia
positions/ethiopian-canon/oneLine: The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church receives 81 books, including 1 Enoch, Jubilees, the Ethiopian books of Meqabyan and, in the broader canon, church-order books such as the Sinodos and Ethiopic Clement.
positions/ethiopian-canon/coreClaims/0: 1 Enoch and Jubilees are inspired Scripture (Jude 14–15 quotes 1 Enoch).
positions/ethiopian-canon/coreClaims/1: The canon of 81 books is counted in a ‘narrower’ form (46 OT + 35 NT including church orders, in some reckonings) and a ‘broader’ form; lists vary.
positions/ethiopian-canon/coreClaims/2: The Ge'ez Bible, translated from the 4th–6th centuries, preserves texts lost elsewhere.
positions/ethiopian-canon/origin: Christianity reached Aksum under Frumentius (c. 330) and King Ezana; Ge'ez translations by the 5th–6th centuries (traditionally the ‘Nine Saints’ from Syria); 1 Enoch and Jubilees survive complete only in Ge'ez.
positions/ethiopian-canon/strongestArgum: 1 Enoch is quoted in Jude and was widely read in Second Temple Judaism and early Christianity (e.g. Epistle of Barnabas, Tertullian).
It preserves an independent, ancient African Christian tradition.
It shows the canon was received in different communities with different breadth.
positions/ethiopian-canon/strongestObjec: Most other churches did not accept Enoch or Jubilees, and some early writers rejected them.
The inclusion of church-order books blurs the line between Scripture and canon law.
The list is not uniform in practice.
positions/ethiopian-canon/responses/0: Ethiopian scholars answer that the canon reflects early Christian usage that other churches later narrowed.
positions/ethiopian-canon/consequences/0: Ethiopia preserved Enoch and Jubilees for world scholarship (European rediscovery via James Bruce, 1773).
positions/ethiopian-canon/consequences/1: A distinctive African biblical heritage shaping Ethiopian liturgy, art and identity.
positions/marriage-sacrament/oneLine: Marriage between baptised Christians is a sacrament: a real participation in the covenant between Christ and the Church, conferring grace and creating a holy bond.
positions/marriage-sacrament/coreClaims/: Christ raised the natural institution of marriage to the dignity of a sacrament (Trent, Session 24).
Ephesians 5:32 calls marriage a "great mystery" (Vulgate sacramentum) signifying Christ and the Church.
In the Latin tradition the spouses are the ministers through their consent; in the Orthodox the priest’s crowning and blessing effect the mystery.
Marriage is ordered to the good of the spouses and the procreation and education of children.
The sacramental bond is permanent (Catholic) or holy and ideally lifelong (Orthodox).
positions/marriage-sacrament/origin: Augustine spoke of the "sacramentum" of marriage (c.401); Peter Lombard (c.1150) listed it among seven sacraments, confirmed at Verona (1184), Lyon (1274), Florence (1439) and Trent (1563). Eastern churches developed the crowning rite and counted marriage among the holy mysteries.
positions/marriage-sacrament/strongestAr: Paul links marriage to the mystery of Christ and the Church in uniquely exalted terms.
Jesus’ presence at Cana and his teaching on "what God hath joined" suggest God himself acts in marriage.
A sacramental view sustains the sanctity and permanence of marriage against purely contractual views.
positions/marriage-sacrament/strongestOb: Reformers argued that marriage, instituted at creation and shared by non-Christians, lacks a specific gospel promise of grace, so it is not a sacrament in the strict sense (Augsburg Apology XIII; Article XXV).
The Vulgate’s "sacramentum" translates mysterion, which does not mean "sacrament" in the later technical sense.
Critics note that the doctrine developed late, in the 12th century.
positions/marriage-sacrament/responses/0: Catholics and Orthodox answer that the development made explicit what was implicit in Scripture and the Fathers.
positions/marriage-sacrament/responses/1: They argue that Christian marriage differs from natural marriage because it is entered "in the Lord" (1 Cor 7:39) and sanctified by grace.
positions/marriage-sacrament/consequence: Church jurisdiction over marriage in medieval and Catholic societies.
Indissolubility and annulment practice in Catholic canon law.
Rich liturgical rites of marriage in East and West.
positions/marriage-covenant-civil/name: Marriage as covenant and civil estate (Protestant)
positions/marriage-covenant-civil/oneLin: Marriage is a holy ordinance of creation and a covenant before God, not a sacrament of the gospel; it belongs to the common life of all humanity and falls under civil as well as church oversight.
positions/marriage-covenant-civil/coreCl: God instituted marriage in Paradise for companionship, procreation and (after the fall) as a remedy against sin.
It is not a sacrament because it carries no specific promise of saving grace and is shared by unbelievers.
It is a covenant made before God and witnesses (Mal 2:14; Prov 2:17).
It is a high calling, equal or superior in dignity to celibacy; clergy may marry.
Civil authorities rightly regulate marriage and divorce.
positions/marriage-covenant-civil/origin: Luther’s Babylonian Captivity (1520) and The Estate of Marriage (1522); Calvin’s Genevan marriage ordinances (1546) and covenantal model; Anglican Prayer Book rite (1549) and Article XXV; Puritan theology of companionate marriage.
positions/marriage-covenant-civil/strong: Marriage is a creation ordinance universal to humanity, not a rite unique to the church.
Scripture calls marriage a covenant (Mal 2:14), a category richer than contract.
Rejecting compulsory celibacy restored the dignity of family life and lay vocation.
Catholic and Orthodox theologians argue it weakens the sacramental and permanent character of marriage, opening the way to divorce and secular redefinition.
Handing marriage to civil authorities has, critics argue, led to the modern state redefining it independently of Christian teaching.
Anglo-Catholics note that Anglican rites still treat marriage sacramentally, showing the line is blurred.
positions/marriage-covenant-civil/respon: Protestants answer that covenant theology grounds permanence and fidelity strongly without sacramental claims.
They argue that Scripture, not church jurisdiction, defines marriage, so Christians can uphold its meaning in any legal order.
positions/marriage-covenant-civil/conseq: Clerical marriage and the Protestant parsonage.
Marriage courts and divorce law move to the state.
positions/clerical-celibacy-latin/oneLin: Priests of the Latin Church should be celibate, freely giving themselves wholly to Christ and his people after the pattern of Christ’s own life, as an ecclesiastical discipline confirmed since the 12th century.
positions/clerical-celibacy-latin/coreCl: Celibacy "for the kingdom of heaven" configures the priest to Christ, the celibate Bridegroom of the Church.
It frees the priest for undivided service (1 Cor 7:32–35).
It is an ancient discipline (Council of Elvira c.305, canon 33, required continence of married clergy) made universal law in the West.
It is a discipline, not a dogma; Eastern Catholic married priests and convert clergy are exceptions.
positions/clerical-celibacy-latin/origin: Early councils (Elvira c.305; Carthage 390) required continence of married clergy in the West; the Gregorian reform (from 1049) campaigned against clerical marriage, and the Second Lateran Council (1139) declared clerical marriages invalid; reaffirmed by Trent (1563), Paul VI (Sacerdotalis Caelibatus, 1967) and Benedict XVI.
positions/clerical-celibacy-latin/strong: Jesus himself was unmarried and commended celibacy for the kingdom; Paul wished all were as he was.
It allows priests to serve with total availability, as in missionary and poor contexts.
It is a powerful eschatological sign that God alone can satisfy the human heart.
Peter was married, and Paul says bishops should be "the husband of one wife" (1 Tim 3:2); the Eastern churches have always had married priests.
Protestant reformers argued that forced celibacy produced widespread concubinage and hypocrisy, against 1 Timothy 4:3.
Some argue it contributes to priest shortages and, in combination with clericalism, to abuse cultures (though studies dispute a causal link).
positions/clerical-celibacy-latin/respon: Defenders answer that the discipline concerns the Latin Church’s chosen ideal and admits exceptions, and that celibacy chosen freely is a gift, not a law imposed on unwilling men.
They point to the Amazon Synod (2019) debate, in which Pope Francis declined to relax the discipline, as evidence of its continuing support.
positions/clerical-celibacy-latin/conseq: A celibate Latin priesthood for nine centuries.
Ongoing debate over ordaining married men (viri probati).
positions/married-clergy/oneLine: Ordained ministers may be married, as the apostles and many early bishops were; celibacy is a gift for some, not a law for all clergy.
positions/married-clergy/coreClaims/0: Peter and other apostles had wives (Mark 1:30; 1 Cor 9:5).
positions/married-clergy/coreClaims/1: Bishops and deacons are to be "the husband of one wife" (1 Tim 3:2, 12).
positions/married-clergy/coreClaims/2: Forbidding marriage is a mark of false teaching (1 Tim 4:3).
positions/married-clergy/coreClaims/3: In Orthodox practice men may marry before ordination as deacon or priest, but not after; bishops are chosen from celibates.
positions/married-clergy/coreClaims/4: Protestant churches allow clergy to marry at any time.
positions/married-clergy/origin: Married clergy were normal in the early church (the tradition of Paphnutius at Nicaea, 325, is legendary but reflects Eastern practice); codified in the East by the Council in Trullo (692); restored in the West by the Reformers (Zwingli, Luther 1525, Cranmer), and permitted in England from 1549.
positions/married-clergy/proponentsOther: Orthodox and Eastern Catholic clergy families
positions/married-clergy/strongestArgume: The New Testament assumes married church leaders.
Married clergy model family life for congregations and avoid the abuses of enforced celibacy.
Eastern churches preserved married priests for two millennia without loss of holiness.
positions/married-clergy/strongestObject: Latin Catholics argue that celibacy better conforms the priest to Christ and frees him for service.
Even in the East, bishops must be celibate, suggesting a recognised higher ideal.
Some argue that family responsibilities limit pastoral availability and mobility.
positions/married-clergy/responses/0: Advocates reply that Scripture prizes marriage and celibacy as different gifts, not ranks.
positions/married-clergy/responses/1: They note that Catholic Eastern rites and the Anglican Ordinariate already include married priests.
positions/married-clergy/consequences/0: The Protestant parsonage and clergy families.
positions/married-clergy/consequences/1: Married parish priests in Orthodoxy and Eastern Catholicism.
positions/catholic-indissolubility-annul: Indissolubility and annulment (Catholic)
Absolute indissolubility
Declaration of nullity
Annulment

A valid, consummated sacramental marriage cannot be dissolved by any human power; divorced people who remarry civilly while a spouse lives are in an objectively irregular situation, though a church tribunal may find that a valid marriage never existed.
Jesus forbade divorce and remarriage as adultery (Mark 10:11–12; Luke 16:18).
Matthew’s "except for porneia" refers to unlawful (e.g. incestuous) unions, not adultery in a valid marriage.
Separation is permitted for grave reasons, but not remarriage.
Nullity may be declared for defects of consent, form or impediments.
Non-sacramental marriages may be dissolved in favour of faith (Pauline and Petrine privileges).

Rooted in the early Western tradition (Hermas, Augustine, Jerome) and canon law; defined at Trent (1563) and codified in the 1917 and 1983 Codes; reaffirmed in Familiaris Consortio (1981); pastoral development in Mitis Iudex (2015) and Amoris Laetitia (2016).

Council of Trent

Walter Kasper (pastoral proposals)
Mark and Luke record Jesus’ prohibition without exception, and Paul repeats it as a command of the Lord (1 Cor 7:10–11).
Indissolubility reflects Christ’s unbreakable covenant with the Church.
It protects spouses and children from abandonment.
Protestants and Orthodox argue that Matthew’s exception and Paul’s desertion clause allow divorce and remarriage.
Critics say annulment can function in practice as "Catholic divorce", especially after procedures were simplified.
Pastorally it can exclude remarried divorcees from communion for life (debated after Amoris Laetitia).
Catholics answer that nullity declares a fact (no valid bond) rather than dissolving one.
Amoris Laetitia (2016) allows case-by-case discernment while keeping the doctrine.
Church tribunals and annulment practice.
Debates over communion for divorced and remarried Catholics.
Catholic opposition to civil divorce laws (e.g. Italy 1974, Ireland 1995 referendums).
